How can you tell if a calorie counting app is really free?

"Free" can be a plan that never expires, a trial that charges you on day eight, or an app that will not scan a barcode until you pay. Seven things to check on the Google Play listing before you install, with our own app as the example and its limits in plain sight.

November 9, 2026 · By Fotocal, Madrid · 6 min read

Part 12 of 12 in Calories, from the ground up

Quick answer: A calorie counting app is truly free when its free plan never expires, asks for no card and lets you log every meal of the day without paying. To find out, check seven things on the Google Play listing and in the app itself: daily limits, whether the trial charges on its own, which basic features are paid, the price, how to cancel and whether you can delete your account.

"Free" is the word calorie apps use most on their listings, and the one that tells you least. It can mean a plan that never expires, a seven-day trial that charges you on day eight, or an app that opens the diary but will not scan a barcode. All three are advertised the same way. The difference is in the small print, and nearly all of it can be read before you install.

Below are the seven things worth checking, in the order you come across them. For each one we use our own app as the example, Fotocal, the photo calorie counter, with its limits in plain sight, so you can compare any other app on the same criteria.

1. What the free plan includes each day

The first question is not whether there is a free plan, but what fits into it on a normal day. Almost every app sets a cap: scans per day, logs per week, days of history. Look for the exact number on the listing or on the app's plans screen. If it is nowhere to be found, be wary: a limit that is not published is usually a small one.

Example, Fotocal: the free plan includes 2 AI scans a day (a photo of the plate), 1 voice log a day, and unlimited barcode scanner and Coach Kal. No card and no expiry date. Two photos a day cover lunch and dinner; breakfast and packaged food go in by barcode or by hand.

2. Whether the free trial charges on its own

A free trial is not a free plan. On Google Play, subscriptions with a trial are charged automatically when the trial ends unless you cancel, and starting a trial needs a payment method on your Google account. Nothing wrong with that, but you should know it: note the day it ends.

Example, Fotocal: the Premium trial lasts 5 days and charges nothing during them. On day six Google Play charges the plan you chose, €6.99 a month or €19.99 a year, unless you have cancelled. Two or three days before the charge, the app sends you a reminder with the date and the amount. The free plan, on the other hand, has no trial and no charge: it is simply free.

3. Whether "free" is a trial that expires

Some apps call the first few days "free". To find out, look on the listing or in the app for the word "trial" and a length of time. If there is one, the free part ends. If what there is is a free plan with limits, you can stay on it indefinitely.

Example, Fotocal: the free plan does not expire. You can use it for months without paying anything; Premium only removes the two daily counters and opens the more detailed panels. The details are on the pricing page.

4. Which basic features are behind the paywall

Counting calories needs three things: logging quickly (photo, barcode, voice or search), seeing the day's total against your target and seeing the macros. If any of those three is paid, the free plan is a sample, not something for every day. Pay special attention to the barcode scanner: it is the most accurate way to log packaged food, and in some apps it is paid.

Example, Fotocal: the free plan has the unlimited barcode scanner, the diary, the calorie target, the macros, water, steps and the weekly report. What is paid are photo scans and voice logs above the daily limit, the full nutrition table in the weekly report and the complete vitamins and minerals panel.

5. The real price, in euros

A Google Play listing flags anything paid with the "In-app purchases" label, but it does not always say how much. The price that matters is the one on the subscription screen before you confirm, and it is worth dividing the yearly price by twelve: it is usually well below the monthly one.

Example, Fotocal: €6.99 a month or €19.99 a year, about €1.67 a month. Both prices are published on the website and are the same in the app.

6. How to cancel

On Android, Google Play subscriptions are cancelled from Google Play, not by deleting the app. Deleting the app cancels nothing. The route is always the same: Play Store app → your profile picture → Payments and subscriptions → Subscriptions → the app → Cancel subscription. You keep what you paid for until the end of the period.

Example, Fotocal: you cancel by that route, and if you do it during the 5-day trial nothing is charged. Google Play does the charging, so refunds are also requested from Google Play.

7. Whether you can delete your account and your data

A calorie app stores what you eat, your weight and sometimes photos of your meals. Google Play requires apps with accounts to let you delete them, and the listing's "Data safety" section says what data is collected and whether it can be deleted. Read it before installing: it is short.

Example, Fotocal: you can delete your account and everything in it from the app, and a page explains how to delete your Fotocal account step by step.

A quick way to compare two apps

Run the same test on both for a week: log everything you eat without paying. At the end, answer three questions: could you log everything? How long did each meal take? Did it ask you to pay for something you needed? The one that passes all three is the one that works for you for free. If weighing food is what puts you off, read how to count calories without weighing every meal, and if you are torn between photo apps, how to choose a photo calorie counter.

And before you start, work out your target: the daily calorie calculator gives you your maintenance and the numbers to lose or gain weight, with the same formula the app uses.

Key points

  • "Free" can be a plan with no end date or a trial that charges on its own: look for the word "trial" and a length of time.
  • What matters is what fits into a free day: scan limits, and whether barcode and macros are included.
  • Google Play subscriptions are cancelled from Google Play; deleting the app cancels nothing.
  • Read the listing's "Data safety" section and check that you can delete your account.
  • Fotocal: free plan with no card and no expiry, with 2 AI scans a day, 1 voice log a day, and unlimited barcode scanner and Coach Kal. Premium: €6.99 a month or €19.99 a year, with a 5-day trial.

Questions people ask

Which calorie counter is free?

Many have a free plan, but with different limits. To compare, check whether the free plan expires, whether it asks for a card, how many logs it allows a day and whether barcode and macros are included. Fotocal has a free plan with no card and no expiry: 2 AI scans a day, 1 voice log a day, and unlimited barcode scanner and Coach Kal.

Is there a completely free calorie counting app?

There are apps with a free plan that never expires and lets you log a whole day, though almost always with some limit. What matters is that the basics (logging, seeing the total and the macros) are not paid. Try a week logging everything without paying: if you can, it is truly free for you.

Will a free trial charge me if I do not cancel?

Yes. On Google Play, subscriptions with a trial are charged automatically when the trial ends unless you cancel. Fotocal's trial lasts 5 days with no charge; on day six Google Play charges €6.99 a month or €19.99 a year, and the app reminds you two or three days before.

Does deleting the app cancel the subscription?

No. Google Play subscriptions are cancelled from the Play Store app: your profile picture → Payments and subscriptions → Subscriptions → the app → Cancel subscription. Deleting the app cancels nothing.

This article is general information, not medical advice.
